To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) loss of MMR enhances the ability of cis-platin to generate variants that are resistant to the topoisomerase I inhibitor topotecan, the nucleoside analog gemcitabine and the microtubule-stabilizing drug paclitaxol; and (2) loss of MNR increases the rate of spontaneous generation of variants resistant only to topotecan.

loss of DNA mismatch-repair function (MMR) in human colon carcinoma cells (HCT116) and human endometrial carcinoma cells (HEC59) enhances the mutagenic effects of cisplatin and increases the frequency of variants that are resistant to three commonly used drugs with which cisptatin is combined in cancer treatment regimens: topotecan, paclitaxal, and gemcitabne.
cisplatin is 2-3-fold more potent at inducing resistance to the drugs gemcitabine and topotecan, and perhaps paclitaxol, in mismatch repair-deficient cells than in mismatch repair-proficient cells.

the role that loss of DNA mismatch (MMR) plays in the development of resistance to anticancer drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the loss of mismatch repair increases the ability of a mutagenic agent to generate variants resistant not only to the agent itself but also to drugs with which the agent is commonly used.

the loss of DNA mismatch-repair (MMR) increases the ability of the DNA-damaging agent cisplatin to select for variants resistant to topoisomerase I (TopoI)-inhibiting, ribonucleotide reductase (RNR)-inhibiting and microtubule-interfering agents, respectively.
MMR deficiency is associated with a higher spontaneous rate of generation and a higher cisplatin-induced rate of generation of resistant cells to topotecan- or gemcitabine-based chemotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
loss of MMR makes cancer cells more resistant to chemotherapy, and that this resistance is not limited to cisplatin, but extends to other commonly used chemotherapeutic drugs.

loss of MMR makes cells more resistant to cisplatin and more likely to develop resistance to other drugs with or without cisplatin.
The main takeaway from our work is that

loss of MMR makes cells more resistant to cisplatin-induced mutagenesis and that the mutagenic activity of cisplatin is not the only factor that determines the frequency of generation of variants that are resistant to other chemotherapeutic drugs.
loss of MMR enhances the ability of cis-platin to generate drug-resistant cells, and this may be one of the reasons why MMR-deficient tumors are more likely to be resistant to chemotherapy.
loss of MMR can increase the likelihood that cisplatin will produce resistant cells.
